lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: # Logic Prototype

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: A tiny interactive terminal app that lets the user drive a state model by hand. Use this when the question is about **business logic, state transitions, or data shape** — the kind of thing that looks reasonable on paper but only feels wrong once you push it through real cases.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ## When this is the right shape

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - "I'm not sure if this state machine handles the edge case where X then Y."

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - "Does this data model actually let me represent the case where..."

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - "I want to feel out what the API should look like before writing it."

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - Anything where the user wants to **press buttons and watch state change**.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: If the question is "what should this look like" — wrong branch. Use [UI.md](UI.md).

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ## Process

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 1. State the question

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Before writing code, write down what state model and what question you're prototyping. One paragraph, in the prototype's README or a comment at the top of the file. A logic prototype that answers the wrong question is pure waste — make the question explicit so it can be checked later, whether the user is watching now or returning to it AFK.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 2. Pick the language

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Use whatever the host project uses. If the project has no obvious runtime (e.g. a docs repo), ask.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Match the project's existing conventions for tooling — don't add a new package manager or runtime just for the prototype.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 3. Isolate the logic in a portable module

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Put the actual logic — the bit that's answering the question — behind a small, pure interface that could be lifted out and dropped into the real codebase later. The TUI around it is throwaway; the logic module shouldn't be.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: The right shape depends on the question:

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **A pure reducer** — `(state, action) => state`. Good when actions are discrete events and state is a single value.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **A state machine** — explicit states and transitions. Good when "which actions are even legal right now" is part of the question.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **A small set of pure functions** over a plain data type. Good when there's no implicit current state — just transformations.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **A class or module with a clear method surface** when the logic genuinely owns ongoing internal state.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Pick whichever shape best fits the question being asked, *not* whichever is easiest to wire to a TUI. Keep it pure: no I/O, no terminal code, no `console.log` for control flow. The TUI imports it and calls into it; nothing flows the other direction.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: This is what makes the prototype useful past its own lifetime. When the question's been answered, the validated reducer / machine / function set can be lifted into the real module — the TUI shell gets deleted.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 4. Build the smallest TUI that exposes the state

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Build it as a **lightweight TUI** — on every tick, clear the screen (`console.clear()` / `print("\033[2J\033[H")` / equivalent) and re-render the whole frame. The user should always see one stable view, not an ever-growing scrollback.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Each frame has two parts, in this order:

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: 1. **Current state**, pretty-printed and diff-friendly (one field per line, or formatted JSON). Use **bold** for field names or section headers and **dim** for less important context (timestamps, IDs, derived values). Native ANSI escape codes are fine — `\x1b[1m` bold, `\x1b[2m` dim, `\x1b[0m` reset. No need to pull in a styling library unless one is already in the project.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: 2. **Keyboard shortcuts**, listed at the bottom: `[a] add user  [d] delete user  [t] tick clock  [q] quit`. Bold the key, dim the description, or vice-versa — whatever reads cleanly.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Behaviour:

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: 1. **Initialise state** — a single in-memory object/struct. Render the first frame on start.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: 2. **Read one keystroke (or one line)** at a time, dispatch to a handler that mutates state.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: 3. **Re-render** the full frame after every action — don't append, replace.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: 4. **Loop until quit.**

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: The whole frame should fit on one screen.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 5. Make it runnable in one command

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Add a script to the project's existing task runner (`package.json` scripts, `Makefile`, `justfile`, `pyproject.toml`). The user should run `pnpm run <prototype-name>` or equivalent — never need to remember a path.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: If the host project has no task runner, just put the command at the top of the prototype's README.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 6. Hand it over

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: Give the user the run command. They'll drive it themselves; the interesting moments are when they say "wait, that shouldn't be possible" or "huh, I assumed X would be different" — those are the bugs in the _idea_, which is the whole point. If they want new actions added, add them. Prototypes evolve.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ### 7. Capture the answer

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: When the prototype has done its job, the answer to the question is the only thing worth keeping. If the user is around, ask what it taught them. If not, leave a `NOTES.md` next to the prototype so the answer can be filled in (or filled in by you, if you've watched the session) before the prototype gets deleted.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: ## Anti-patterns

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **Don't add tests.** A prototype that needs tests is no longer a prototype.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **Don't wire it to the real database.** Use an in-memory store unless the question is specifically about persistence.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **Don't generalise.** No "what if we wanted to support X later." The prototype answers one question.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **Don't blur the logic and the TUI together.** If the reducer / state machine references `console.log`, prompts, or terminal escape codes, it's no longer portable. Keep the TUI as a thin shell over a pure module.

lines.author: matemolnar8
lines.text: - **Don't ship the TUI shell into production.** The shell is optimised for being driven by hand from a terminal. The logic module behind it is the bit worth keeping.
